title: The Holy Spirit and the church
for: I want to know what the Spirit and the church are
subtitle: Eleven sessions on who the Holy Spirit is and what he does, and on what the church is, how it is ordered and why it is sent, traced to Scripture and the creeds.
intro: The creeds confess the Holy Spirit and the church in neighboring lines, and the order is not an accident. The church is what the Spirit makes: a people born again, gathered, gifted and sent. These eleven sessions take the Spirit first, as a person and as God, through the Old Testament and Pentecost into the life of a believer, and then the church, from what it is to how it is ordered and why it exists.

Each session aims to leave you able to state the doctrine in your own words, show it in Scripture, say why the church holds it, and explain it simply to someone else. The Spirit's deity and personhood are confessed plainly. On the gifts, baptism, the Supper and church government, faithful Christians differ, and each view is given in its strongest voice and left open. LiveWell is written by a Baptist pastor, and where that matters the track says so without arguing for it.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a group through The Holy Spirit and the church. It suits believers who want to understand the Spirit's work and their own congregation better, and it suits people from different churches studying together, because several sessions take up questions on which their churches differ. The leader's task is to keep the group in Scripture, to confess plainly what the creeds confess, and to let each tradition be heard in its own voice.

Each person reads the session, opens its page and does what it asks before the group meets. The meeting doesn't repeat the teaching. It talks over what people found, and it gives someone the chance each week to explain the doctrine aloud in their own words.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, weekly or fortnightly, for eleven meetings, and keep the end time you promised. A group drawn from more than one church is a gift for this track, because the sessions on the gifts, the signs and church government are best heard from people who practice them differently. A leader doesn't need to be a theologian, only to have done the reading and to be willing to say when they don't know.

sections.title: The room
body: A table works best, with Bibles open in print or on a phone, and paper for notes. Say at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that members will disagree about some things and remain brothers and sisters, and that no one has to pray aloud. What people say about their own lives and their own churches stays in the room, unless someone is in danger.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Ten minutes: one person reads the verse aloud with the passage around it, while the others follow.
Thirty minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Where churches differ, let each view be stated by someone who holds it, or as its defenders would.
Ten minutes: two people explain the session's doctrine in their own words, as if to a friend who has never heard it.
Ten minutes: what each person did with the session's task, and one question it raised.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt, in the group's own words, and the date of the next meeting.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Ask first what order the question is. That the Spirit is a person and is God, that he gives new birth, and that the church is one body under Christ are first-order, and the sessions say so plainly. Whether the extraordinary gifts continue, who should be baptized, what happens at the Supper and how a church is governed divide faithful churches but not the faith. Leave those open, and don't let the group become a contest between traditions.

If someone describes an experience of the Spirit others in the room have never had, listen before anyone weighs it. If no one knows the answer to a question, write it down and bring it back the next week.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Sessions about the church will bring up churches that hurt people. Someone may have been shamed in a meeting, pushed to perform a gift, disciplined harshly, or harmed by a leader. When that happens, stop and listen. Thank them for saying it, don't defend the church that hurt them, and don't hurry back to the outline. Speak with them on their own afterwards.

If someone says that a leader or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret. Abuse of a child is a matter for the authorities, never something a church handles quietly.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has grown too heavy to set down: harm done to them in a church or at home, guilt or fear that will not let them rest, grief that has taken their sleep for weeks, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, among them help for church hurt, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor.

sessions.title: The Spirit as a person and as God
teaching: Many Christians speak of the Holy Spirit as a force, an influence or a feeling. Scripture will not let him be an it. He teaches and reminds: “the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name, will teach you all things” (John 14:26). He speaks, setting apart Barnabas and Saul for their work. He prays for believers “with groans too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). And he can be grieved. A force cannot be grieved. A person can, and only one who loves.

He is also God. When Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit, Peter told him he had lied to God. Jesus sends his disciples to baptize in one name, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. In the fourth century some taught that the Spirit was a created power, and Athanasius and Basil answered them: only God can give divine life and make people holy. The Council of Constantinople in 381 confessed him the Lord and giver of life, worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son. This is first-order. Whether he proceeds from the Father alone, or from the Father and the Son, divides East and West, and the Study Bible gives both sides.

open.label: Who is the Holy Spirit?
open.why: The Spirit's person and deity, with every view the church weighed stated in its own voice and the reasons the councils gave.

also.label: The Nicene Creed
also.why: The creed of 381 that confesses the Spirit as the Lord and giver of life, with notes on the words added at Constantinople.

also.label: The Holy Spirit, in the Study Bible
also.why: The Spirit traced from creation to Revelation, with the Eastern and Western confessions of his procession set side by side.

sessions.question: Do you more naturally think of the Holy Spirit as a power or as a person, and what difference would the other make?
sessions.do: Read John 14:15-26 and Acts 5:1-4. List every personal thing the Spirit does in them, and then explain in two sentences why Christians say he is God.

verse.text: And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

group.open: What were you taught about the Holy Spirit growing up, if anything?
discuss: Why does it matter that the Spirit can be grieved?
What did the church see at stake in confessing the Spirit as God and not a created power?
How would you explain to a friend that the Spirit is a person without making him sound like a ghost?
group.pray: Thank the Father for the gift of the Spirit, and ask the Spirit to teach the group what the Son has said.

sessions.title: The Spirit in the Old Testament
teaching: The Spirit does not arrive at Pentecost. He is there in the Bible's second verse: “the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters” (Genesis 1:2). Through the Old Testament he gives life, and he comes on particular people for particular work. He fills Bezalel with skill to build the tabernacle. He comes upon judges like Gideon and kings like Saul and David. He speaks through the prophets. David, after his great fall, prays: “take not Your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 51:11). The Spirit came on some, for a task, and sometimes for a time.

That limit became a longing and then a promise. When others prophesied in the camp, Moses said he wished all the LORD's people were prophets. Ezekiel heard God promise a new heart and his own Spirit within his people, and saw a valley of dry bones stand up when the breath of God came into them. Joel heard of a day when the Spirit would be poured out on all people, sons and daughters, old and young. The Old Testament closes with the promise still open. Its readers knew what the Spirit could do. They were waiting for him to be given to everyone.

open.label: The Holy Spirit through the Bible
open.why: A short film following the Spirit from the waters of creation through the judges and prophets to the promise of a Spirit poured out on all.

also.label: Ezekiel 36, passage by passage

also.label: Numbers 11, passage by passage

also.label: Study a Bible word
also.why: Look up ruach, the Hebrew word for breath, wind and spirit, and see the verses where it appears across the Old Testament.

sessions.question: What is the difference between the Spirit coming upon a few people for a task and the Spirit poured out on all?
sessions.do: Read Ezekiel 36:24-28 and Joel 2:28-29. Write down, in your own words, what God promised his Spirit would do, and for whom.

verse.text: And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes and to carefully observe My ordinances.

group.open: Where in the Old Testament, if anywhere, had you noticed the Spirit before?
discuss: Why might David have prayed so urgently not to lose the Spirit in Psalm 51?
What was Moses longing for in Numbers 11, and how was his wish answered?
How does the promise in Ezekiel 36 change what you expect the Spirit to do in a believer?
group.pray: Ask God to give his people new hearts, and give thanks that the promise made through Ezekiel and Joel has been kept.

sessions.title: Pentecost
teaching: Pentecost was a feast before it was a Christian one. It was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, when Jerusalem filled with pilgrims from across the known world. On that day the disciples were together when a sound like rushing wind filled the house: “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them” (Acts 2:4). The crowd heard the wonders of God in their own languages. Peter told them what they were seeing: Joel's promise kept, and the risen Jesus, exalted to God's right hand, pouring out the Spirit.

Many readers have seen at Pentecost the undoing of Babel, where one language became many and the peoples scattered. Here many languages carry one message, and the scattered are gathered. Christians agree that Pentecost was a turning point, the Spirit given to the whole church. They differ on what it means for believers since. Pentecostal Christians teach a baptism in the Spirit after conversion, often marked by tongues, which empowers for witness. Most other traditions read Spirit baptism as part of coming to faith, with many fillings to follow. Both read Acts with care. The question is second-order, and it stays open here.

also.label: The first Christians

sessions.question: Why do you think God chose a pilgrim feast, with many languages in the city, for the day the Spirit was given?

verse.text: Exalted, then, to the right hand of God, He has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear.

group.open: What comes to mind when you hear the word Pentecostal?

How do Pentecostal and other Christians each read Acts 2, stated at their strongest?
What would a church look like that took seriously that the Spirit was given to all of it?
group.pray: Give thanks for the gift of the Spirit to the whole church, and pray for believers who worship in other languages and lands.

sessions.title: New birth, indwelling and assurance
teaching: No one becomes a Christian by trying harder. Jesus told Nicodemus, a respected teacher, that he must be born of water and the Spirit, and that the Spirit moves like the wind, unseen but known by what he does. The new birth is the Spirit giving life to someone who could not give it to themselves. Then he stays. Paul says that whoever belongs to Christ has the Spirit of Christ living in them, that a believer's body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and that believers are sealed with the Spirit as a pledge of what is still to come.

The Spirit also gives assurance: “The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children” (Romans 8:16). That is not a mood. It is the quiet confidence to call God Father, joined to a life he is slowly changing. Christians differ on the order of these things. The Reformed tradition holds that the new birth comes before faith and makes it possible. Wesleyan and Arminian Christians hold that grace goes before every person, and that faith receives the new birth. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and many Anglican Christians tie the new birth to baptism. Baptists have held both of the first two. All agree that salvation is the Spirit's work from first to last.

also.label: John 3, passage by passage

also.label: Romans 8, passage by passage

also.label: Union with Christ, in the Study Bible

sessions.question: What would you say to a believer who wants to know whether the Spirit really lives in them?
sessions.do: Read John 3:1-8 and Romans 8:9-17. Then explain the new birth to a friend in plain words, without using the phrase born again.

verse.text: The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children.

care: If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What did the phrase born again mean to you before you read John 3?

How do the Reformed and Wesleyan accounts of the new birth differ, and what do they share?
Where does assurance come from, if it is not a feeling?
group.pray: Give thanks for the Spirit who gives life, and pray for anyone in the group who struggles to believe that God calls them his child.

sessions.title: The fruit of the Spirit
teaching: Paul does not give a list of virtues to achieve. He describes a harvest: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23). The word is fruit, not fruits, as if the nine were one life seen from nine sides. Fruit is not manufactured. It grows from a living root over seasons. That is why the fruit is a surer sign of the Spirit's presence than any gift. A gifted person can be cruel. A loving one cannot.

Growth is still not passive. In the same chapter Paul sets the fruit against the works of the flesh, and he tells believers to keep in step with the Spirit. The church calls this sanctification: God making his people holy through the means he has given, the Scriptures, prayer, the Lord's Table and the company of other believers. Christians differ on how complete that holiness can become in this life, and the Study Bible sets out the views. They agree that it is slow, that it is real, and that it begins with love.

sessions.question: Which part of the fruit of the Spirit is slowest to grow in you, and what might be crowding it out?
sessions.do: Read Galatians 5:13-26. Choose one part of the fruit, and for a week notice each time you are given a chance to show it. Write down what happened.

verse.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

group.open: Who is someone you know whose life shows the fruit of the Spirit?
discuss: Why might Paul speak of one fruit rather than nine virtues?
What is the difference between trying to be patient and the Spirit growing patience in you?
Why might the fruit be a surer sign of the Spirit than the gifts?
group.pray: Ask the Spirit to grow his fruit in each person, naming the part each one most needs.

sessions.title: The gifts of the Spirit
teaching: Every believer is gifted. Paul's rule covers them all: “to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:7). Some gifts look ordinary: teaching, serving, giving, leading and mercy. Others are plainly extraordinary: prophecy, tongues, healing and miracles. Scripture never ranks the first kind as less spiritual. And Paul sets his chapter on love between his two chapters on gifts, so that no one forgets that a gift without love is only noise. The gifts are for others. A gift used to raise yourself up has been misused, however real it is.

Faithful Christians differ on whether the extraordinary gifts continue. Cessationists hold that prophecy and tongues belonged to the church's founding, laid once like a foundation, and that Scripture is now sufficient. Continuationists answer that nothing in the New Testament says these gifts would end before Christ returns, and that Paul told the church to desire them. Between them stand many who are open but cautious, and beyond them Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, now a large share of the world's church. Baptists are found across this range. The question is second-order. Each side, at its best, tests everything and holds fast to love.

sessions.do: Read 1 Corinthians 12:4-11 and 13:1-7. Ask two people who know you well what they think you are gifted to do for others, and write down what they say.

sessions.title: The people of God and the body of Christ
teaching: The church is not first a building or a service. It is a people. From the call of Abraham, God's purpose was never only to rescue scattered individuals but to form a community that belongs to him. The New Testament word ekklesia was the ordinary Greek word for an assembly, and the Greek translation of the Old Testament had used it for Israel gathered before God. Peter takes the words spoken to Israel at Sinai and gives them to a church of Jews and Gentiles: “you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession” (1 Peter 2:9).

Paul's picture is a body: “Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it” (1 Corinthians 12:27). Christ is the head, the members need one another, and the weaker members are the ones Paul calls indispensable. The church is universal, every believer in every age, and it is local, the congregation down your street. Augustine called the church on earth a mixed body, wheat and weeds together until the harvest. Christians differ on how visible the church's unity must be, and the Study Bible lets each tradition speak. They agree that no one can belong to the head and despise the body.

sessions.title: The marks of a true church
teaching: How do you know a true church when you see one? The creed gives four marks: one, holy, catholic and apostolic. One, because there is one Lord and one body. Holy, because God has set it apart, not because its members are finished. Catholic, meaning whole and universal, not confined to one people or place. Apostolic, because it stands on the apostles' teaching. Every major tradition still confesses these four, though each reads them differently. The first church in Jerusalem shows them in miniature: “They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer” (Acts 2:42).

The Reformation asked a sharper question, because rival churches each claimed the four. The Augsburg Confession of 1530 named the church where the gospel is purely taught and the sacraments rightly administered. Calvin held to those two marks, and the Belgic Confession of 1561 added church discipline as a third. These marks do not measure size, style or success. They ask whether Christ is preached, whether his signs are kept as he gave them, and whether the church cares enough about holiness to correct itself. Some churches have failed them and done great harm. That is reason to tell the truth, not to give up on the church.

sessions.title: Baptism and the Lord's Supper
teaching: Jesus gave his church two practices it has kept in every century and land. In baptism a person is washed with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit and marked as belonging to Christ. In the Lord's Supper his people eat the bread and drink the cup, remembering him, sharing in him and in one another, and looking for his return. Both are signs he commanded, not inventions of the church. And both gather a people, not only individuals: “Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

Christians differ on what these signs do and to whom they are given. Catholic and Orthodox Christians call them sacraments that truly give the grace they signify, and confess that the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood. Lutherans confess his true body and blood present in, with and under the bread and wine. Reformed Christians speak of a real spiritual feeding by faith, and baptize the infants of believers as members of the covenant. Baptists baptize those who profess faith, by immersion, and many call the Supper an ordinance of remembrance and communion. LiveWell is written by a Baptist pastor. Each view is stated here as its defenders would state it, and left open.

sessions.do: Read Romans 6:1-11 and 1 Corinthians 11:23-26. Then explain to a friend, in plain words, what all Christians share about these two signs and where they part.

sessions.title: Church government and membership
teaching: Every church is governed somehow, and the New Testament names its servants: elders, also called overseers and shepherds, who teach and watch over the flock, and deacons, who serve. Three forms of government have grown from those texts. Episcopal churches are led by bishops in succession from the apostles. Presbyterian churches are led by elders, joined in councils beyond the congregation. Congregational churches hold that each congregation under Christ governs itself, with the elders and deacons it recognizes. Each reads the same passages with care, and the question is second-order. LiveWell is written by a Baptist pastor, and Baptist churches are congregational.

Membership is the church's way of saying who belongs, so that it can care for them. The New Testament assumes believers can be named and counted, and tells leaders to watch over souls as those who must give an account. That watching includes correction. Jesus taught a patient path for a brother who will not turn: privately, then with witnesses, then before the church. Church discipline has been abused, and the harm is real. Done as Jesus taught it, it is love that refuses to let someone wander unnoticed. Joining a church is a promise to be known, and to know others.

sessions.question: What would it cost you to be fully known by a congregation, and what might you gain?
sessions.do: Read 1 Peter 5:1-5 and Hebrews 13:17. If you belong to a church, find out how it is governed and who your leaders are. If you don't, write down what keeps you from joining one.

verse.text: And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.

care: A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Have you ever formally joined a church, and what did it mean to you, or why not?
discuss: What does each form of church government, at its best, protect?
Why might membership be an act of love and not only of organization?
How can a church practice correction without becoming harsh or controlling?
group.pray: Pray for the leaders of your churches, and for anyone who has been wounded by leaders who misused their place.

sessions.title: The church's mission
teaching: The church does not so much have a mission as belong to one. The Father sent the Son, and the Son sends his people: “As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you” (John 20:21). Before he ascended, Jesus told the disciples to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching them, and promised that the Spirit would make them his witnesses to the ends of the earth. Mission is not a program for the keen few. It is what the Spirit-filled church is, wherever it is planted.

Christians have long argued over word and deed. Some insist that proclamation comes first, because no one can believe in one they have not heard of. Others insist that the gospel of the kingdom must be seen in justice and mercy, or it will not be believed. Both draw on Scripture, and most churches hold both. Lesslie Newbigin argued that the best explanation of the gospel a town will ever see is a congregation that believes it and lives by it. The faith has moved south and east, and missionaries now go out from every continent. The commission has not changed. It has always been carried by ordinary people to the streets they already live on.

sessions.question: Who are the people you already live and work among who have never heard the gospel explained well?
sessions.do: Read Matthew 28:16-20 and Acts 1:6-8. Write down the names of three people you see each week, and pray for each by name every day this week.

group.open: Who first explained the gospel to you, and how did they do it?
discuss: Why does it matter that mission begins with God sending, not with the church planning?
